newsitem.title: UK: U.S. may be in for another dustbowl, experts warn.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may be in for another dustbowl, experts warn.

text.p: Severe droughts like the one that created the "dustbowl" of Oklahoma may be rare in North America, but global warming could change that, Canadian climatologists warned on Wednesday.

They said fossilised plankton from the Northern Plains showed that big droughts used to be more severe and more common than they are now, and global warming could shepherd in a return to those bad old days.

Kathleen Laird of Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario and colleagues analysed fossilised diatoms -- tiny algae that live in lakes. Their analysis showed that the climate over the past 500 years has been unusually stable.

"This record...suggests that extreme droughts of greater intensity than that of the 1930s were more frequent before AD 1200. This high frequency of extreme droughts persisted for centuries," they wrote in the science journal Nature.

"Current climate models suggest that increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations could cause an intensification of the extremes of the hydrological cycle, thereby increasing the frequency and severity of floods and droughts," they added.
"A return to the earlier mode of climate variability in the Northern Great Plains before AD 1200 would be devastating."
